title: Interest (SI & CI)
summary: Simple and compound interest — a near-certain slot in every shift. Tier 1 favourites: direct SI, amount at CI with clean chips, CI–SI differences and doubling chains. Tier 2 adds instalments and multi-year rate cases. Everything runs on the multiplier-chip habit.

subtopics.title: Simple Interest
subtopics.concept:
In simple interest the interest every year is a fixed slice of the original principal only.

$$SI = \frac{P \times R \times T}{100}, \qquad A = P + SI$$

Any one of P, R, T, SI can be recovered from the other three. Amount-based questions: first get SI = A − P.

**Growth is linear** at SI: the amount grows by the same rupee amount every year. If a sum becomes n times in T years, the rate is $\frac{100(n-1)}{T}$.

**Instalment intuition at SI:** the borrower pays interest only for the period each part of the money actually stayed with the lender.

tricks.title: Flip the formula, don't solve equations
tricks.body: Write SI = PRT/100 and cover the unknown — that IS the equation.

example.q: Find the simple interest on ₹5,000 at 8% p.a. for 3 years.

tricks.title: n-times ⇄ rate at SI
tricks.body: 'Becomes n times in T years' means interest earned = (n−1)P.

example.q: At what rate per cent per annum will a sum of money double itself in 10 years at simple interest?

tricks.title: SI per year is constant
tricks.body: Divide the total interest by the number of years; everything else follows.

example.q: The simple interest on a sum at 4% p.a. is $\frac{2}{5}$ of the principal. Find the time.

mistakes: Using the amount A as principal in the SI formula (SI is always on the original P).
For 'becomes n times', using n instead of n − 1 in the interest.
Forgetting to convert months to years ($T = 9/12$) or paise-paise rate mix-ups.
Adding SI of different sums without weighting by their time periods.
subtopics.notes:
### What interest is
When you borrow money, you pay a charge for using it; when you lend or deposit, you earn it. That charge is **interest**. The money borrowed or invested is the **principal (P)**, the charge is a per-cent per year called the **rate (R% per annum)**, and the period is the **time (T, in years)**.

### Simple interest — the formula and its four faces
In simple interest (SI) the interest each year is a fixed slice of the **original** principal only. The earlier interest earns nothing more.
$$SI = \frac{P \times R \times T}{100}$$
Keep the units straight: T in years (8 months $= \frac{8}{12} = \frac{2}{3}$ year), R per year. Any one of P, R, T, SI can be found from the other three:
$$P = \frac{100 \times SI}{RT}, \quad R = \frac{100 \times SI}{PT}, \quad T = \frac{100 \times SI}{PR}$$
SI on ₹6,500 at 8% for 3 years: $\frac{6500 \times 8 \times 3}{100} = ₹1{,}560$.

### Amount
**Amount (A)** = what you finally get back or owe: $A = P + SI$. Amount questions: first get SI $= A - P$, then use the formula.
A sum amounts to ₹1,560 in 2 years at 5%: SI $= 1560 - P$ and SI $= \frac{P \times 5 \times 2}{100} = 0.1P$ → $1.1P = 1560$ → P $= ₹1{,}418.18$ — exam numbers are chosen cleaner: A ₹1,540 → P ₹1,400.

### Growth is LINEAR at SI
The amount grows by the same rupee amount every year, so the yearly amounts form an arithmetic progression. Two consequences:
- **n times in T years**: if a sum becomes n times in T years, the interest earned is $(n-1)P$, so
$$R = \frac{100(n-1)}{T}$$
Doubles in 8 years → $\frac{100}{8} = 12.5\%$. Triples in 16 → $\frac{200}{16} = 12.5\%$.
- **T from n and R**: $T = \frac{100(n-1)}{R}$. "In what time will a sum become 5 times at 12%?" → $\frac{400}{12} = 33\frac{1}{3}$ years.
The word "amounts to n times" includes the principal, so the interest part is only $(n-1)$ times P — the classic trap is using n instead of n−1.

### Fraction-of-principal questions
"The SI is $\frac{1}{5}$ of the sum at 4% — find the time." Write $\frac{PRT}{100} = \frac{P}{5}$ → $T = \frac{100}{5 \times 4} = 5$ years. The P cancels; only the fraction, R and T matter.
Same shape: "In what time will the SI be $\frac{2}{9}$ of P at 8%?" → $T = \frac{200}{9 \times 8} = 2\frac{7}{9}$ years.

### Money scaling and comparison
SI is directly proportional to P, R and T. Doubling the sum doubles the interest; halving the rate halves it; the interest on 2P at half the rate equals the original interest.
Difference questions subtract two SI computations, or use ratios: SI on 3P at r% : SI on 2P at 2r% $= 3 : 4$.

### Where the marks are lost
- Mixing months and years (R is per annum; convert months to a fraction of a year).
- Using n instead of n−1 in n-times questions.
- Dividing by the amount when the question gives SI, or the reverse.

### Quick revision
- $SI = \frac{PRT}{100}$; $A = P + SI$; solve for any missing input.
- n times in T years at SI: $R = \frac{100(n-1)}{T}$, $T = \frac{100(n-1)}{R}$.
- Growth is linear: equal rupee growth every year.
- Fraction of P as SI: $T = \frac{100 \times \text{fraction}}{R}$.
- Months to years: divide by 12.

patterns.name: Direct simple interest
patterns.howToSpot: P, R and T are given and the SI (or the amount) is asked directly.
patterns.logic:
1. Convert T to years (months ÷ 12).
2. Multiply P × R × T and divide by 100.
3. For the amount, add P to the SI.

Why: SI is a fixed fraction of the principal every year.

example.q: Find the simple interest on ₹6,500 at 8% per annum for 3 years.

patterns.name: Find P, R or T from the interest or amount
patterns.howToSpot: Three of P, R, T, SI (or A) are given; the fourth is asked.
patterns.formula: P = \frac{100 \times SI}{RT}, \quad R = \frac{100 \times SI}{PT}, \quad T = \frac{100 \times SI}{PR}
patterns.logic:
1. If an amount is given, first take SI = A − P.
2. Rearrange $SI = \frac{PRT}{100}$ for the missing input.
3. Amount-only version: $A = P\left(1 + \frac{RT}{100}\right)$ — one linear equation.

Why: the four quantities are linked by one formula, so any three fix the fourth.

example.q: At what rate per cent per annum will ₹1,250 amount to ₹2,000 in 12 years at simple interest?

patterns.name: n times in T years (doubling, tripling)
patterns.howToSpot: 'A sum doubles / triples / becomes n times itself in T years — find the rate or time.'
patterns.logic:
1. Interest earned = (n − 1) × P — subtract the principal once.
2. Rate: $\frac{100(n-1)}{T}$; Time: $\frac{100(n-1)}{R}$.
3. Chain: doubling in T means tripling in 2T, quadrupling in 3T (linear growth).

Why: 'becomes n times' gives SI = (n−1)P, and P cancels out.

example.q: A sum of money triples itself in 16 years at simple interest. The rate per annum is:

patterns.name: Interest as a fraction of the principal
patterns.howToSpot: 'The SI is 1/5 (or 2/9 …) of the sum after T years at R%' — find T or R.
patterns.logic:
1. Set the fraction equal to $\frac{PRT}{100}$.
2. Cancel P from both sides.
3. Solve for the missing variable.

Why: the principal is common to both sides, so it never enters the answer.

example.q: The simple interest on a sum at 4% per annum is $\frac{1}{5}$ of the sum. The number of years is:

patterns.name: Comparing two SI situations
patterns.howToSpot: Two principals, rates or times are compared — 'how much more interest', or SI on a scaled sum.
patterns.logic:
1. SI is proportional to each of P, R, T — build the ratio.
2. For a difference, compute the two SIs and subtract.
3. 'Double P, half R' leaves SI unchanged (2 × ½ = 1).

Why: the formula is a product, so scaling factors multiply.

subtopics.title: Compound Interest
subtopics.concept:
Compound interest adds each year's interest to the principal — the amount grows **geometrically**.

$$A = P\left(1 + \frac{R}{100}\right)^T, \qquad CI = A - P$$

**Effective multipliers:** 10% → ×11/10, 20% → ×6/5, 4% → ×26/25. Chain the multipliers instead of using the formula blindly.

**Different rate each year** (or gain then loss): multiply the year-wise factors: $A = P\left(1+\frac{r_1}{100}\right)\left(1+\frac{r_2}{100}\right)\cdots$

**Fraction rates** become easy through approximations: $6\tfrac{2}{3}\% = \frac{1}{15}$, so 2 years at CI multiplies the money by $\frac{16}{15} \times \frac{16}{15}$.

tricks.title: Multiplier chips
tricks.body: One chip per year; multiply. For fraction rates pick chips that cancel.

example.q: Find the amount on ₹10,000 at 10% p.a. compound interest for 2 years.

tricks.title: Recover P by dividing the chip
tricks.body: If the amount after T years is known, divide by the chip chain to get the principal.

example.q: A sum amounts to ₹4,840 in 2 years at 10% p.a. CI. Find the sum.

tricks.title: Half-yearly: halve the rate, double the count
tricks.body: Convert the problem, then run the chips.

example.q: Find the CI on ₹8,000 at 20% p.a. for 1$\frac{1}{2}$ years, compounded half-yearly.

mistakes: Compounding $\left(1 + \frac{R}{100}\right)^T$ when the rates differ year to year — multiply factors instead.
For half-yearly compounding, halving the time instead of the rate.
Reporting the amount A when the question asks for CI (or the reverse).
Using $\frac{R}{200}$ but forgetting the exponent $2T$ (or vice versa).
subtopics.notes:
### What compounding means
In **compound interest (CI)**, each year's interest is added to the principal before the next year's interest is worked out. The interest earns interest, so the amount grows **geometrically** — by the same *factor* each year, not the same rupees.
$$A = P\left(1 + \frac{R}{100}\right)^T, \qquad CI = A - P$$

### Multipliers (chips) — the everyday method
Write $1 + \frac{R}{100}$ as a fraction and multiply it T times:
| Rate | Chip |
|---|---|
| 10% | $\frac{11}{10}$ |
| 20% | $\frac{6}{5}$ |
| $12\frac{1}{2}\%$ | $\frac{9}{8}$ |
| $6\frac{1}{4}\%$ | $\frac{17}{16}$ |
| 8% | $\frac{27}{25}$ |
CI on ₹12,000 at 10% for 2 years: $12000 \times \frac{11}{10} \times \frac{11}{10} = ₹14{,}520$ → CI $= ₹2{,}520$.

### The net-effect percentages
Two years at R% → net factor $\left(1+\frac{R}{100}\right)^2$: 10% → 21% (not 20%); 20% → 44%; 25% → 56.25%; 5% → 10.25%.
Three years at 10% → 33.1%; at 20% → 72.8%. These small tables answer "find the amount as % of P" questions instantly.
A 12.5% rate is $\frac{1}{8}$: two years multiply by $\frac{81}{64}$ → amount $= \frac{81}{64}P$, CI $= \frac{17}{64}P$. Fraction chips keep everything exact — prefer them to decimals.

### Fractional years and broken periods
$2\frac{1}{2}$ years at R% (annual compounding) = 2 full years by chips, then **simple interest for the half year** on the amount:
₹10,000 at 10% for $2\frac{1}{2}$ years → $10000 \times 1.1 \times 1.1 = 12{,}100$; half-year SI on it $= 12100 \times \frac{5}{100} = 605$ → ₹12,705.
(Compounded half-yearly instead? See the half-yearly pattern — different answer, different question.)

### Compounding more than once a year
- **Half-yearly**: rate halves, periods double: $A = P\left(1 + \frac{R}{200}\right)^{2T}$.
- **Quarterly**: rate quarters, periods quadruple: $A = P\left(1 + \frac{R}{400}\right)^{4T}$.
₹10,000 at 20% p.a. half-yearly for $1\frac{1}{2}$ years → 3 half-years at 10%: $10000 \times 1.1^3 = ₹13{,}310$.
More frequent compounding always gives more interest than annual compounding at the same nominal rate.

### Different rates in different years
Multiply the year-wise chips: $A = P\left(1+\frac{r_1}{100}\right)\left(1+\frac{r_2}{100}\right)\cdots$
₹25,000 with 10% then 20%: $25000 \times 1.1 \times 1.2 = ₹33{,}000$. A year of gain and a year of loss simply use their own chips.

### Scaling and finding P
CI is proportional to P (same rate and time): CI on ₹30,000 = 1.5 × CI on ₹20,000.
From an amount: divide by the chips. ₹6,655 after 3 years at 10% → $\frac{6655}{1.331} = ₹5{,}000$.

### Quick revision
- $A = P(1 + R/100)^T$; multiply chips T times.
- Net %: 2 years at 10% → 21%; at 20% → 44%; 3 years at 10% → 33.1%.
- Half-yearly: R/2, 2T. Quarterly: R/4, 4T.
- Broken period: full years by chips, then SI on the amount.
- Different yearly rates: multiply their chips.

patterns.name: Amount or CI by the multiplier method
patterns.howToSpot: P, R and whole-year T are given; the amount or CI is asked.
patterns.logic:
1. Write the chip $1 + \frac{R}{100}$ as a small fraction.
2. Multiply P by the chip T times.
3. CI = A − P.

Why: each year scales the running total by the same factor.

example.q: Find the compound interest on ₹12,000 at 10% per annum for 2 years.

patterns.name: Net per cent / fraction-rate compounding
patterns.howToSpot: 'A sum becomes 1.21 times in 2 years' or 'CI as a per cent of P' — the net effect of compounding.
patterns.logic:
1. Square the chip for 2 years, cube it for 3.
2. Read the percentage: 10% → 21%, 20% → 44%, 12.5% → 26.5625% ($\frac{81}{64}$).
3. For a given multiple, take the square root: 1.44 → chip 1.2 → 20%.

Why: compounding applies the same growth twice, so the effects multiply.

example.q: A sum invested at compound interest becomes 1.44 times itself in 2 years. The annual rate is:

patterns.name: Half-yearly or quarterly compounding
patterns.howToSpot: 'Compounded half-yearly / quarterly' appears in the question — usually for $1$ to $2$ years.
patterns.logic:
1. Halve (or quarter) the rate and double (quadruple) the number of periods.
2. Work the periods with chips as usual.
3. Watch $1\frac{1}{2}$ years: half-yearly means 3 periods.

Why: each compounding period uses the rate for that fraction of a year.

example.q: Find the CI on ₹10,000 at 20% per annum for 1½ years, compounded half-yearly.

patterns.name: Different rates in different years
patterns.howToSpot: '8% in the first year and 10% in the second, compounded annually' — sometimes a loss year too.
patterns.logic:
1. Write each year's own chip.
2. Multiply them all with P.
3. CI = A − P (or compare with another scenario).

Why: each year compounds on the running amount at its own rate.

example.q: ₹25,000 is invested at 10% for the first year and 20% for the second, compounded annually. The amount is:

patterns.name: Scaling the CI (same rate, proportional principal)
patterns.howToSpot: The CI for one sum is given; the CI for another sum at the same rate and time is asked.
patterns.logic:
1. CI is proportional to P at fixed rate and time.
2. Ratio the principals; scale the CI.
3. For a changed time, apply the net-per-cent of the new period instead.

Why: every term of the CI formula is linear in P.

example.q: The CI on ₹20,000 for 2 years at 10% is ₹4,200. The CI on ₹30,000 for the same period and rate is:

subtopics.title: CI vs SI: differences & doubling
subtopics.concept:
The extra money CI earns over SI comes from **interest on interest**:

- 2 years: $CI - SI = P\left(\dfrac{R}{100}\right)^2$ — the first year's interest, again at rate R, for one year.
- 3 years: $CI - SI = P\left(\dfrac{R}{100}\right)^2\left(3 + \dfrac{R}{100}\right)$.

**Doubling time at CI:** rate ≈ $\frac{72}{T}$ (rule of 72); exactly, $T = \log 2 \,/\, \log(1 + r/100)$.

**Doubling/tripling chains:** if a sum doubles in T years at CI it becomes $2^k$ times in $kT$ years (4× in 2T, 8× in 3T). Same logic at SI: extra multiples need the same *linear* pace — n times in T ⇒ (n′ − 1) = (n − 1)·T′/T.

formulas.name: SI multiple pace
formulas.tex: n\times \text{ in } T \Rightarrow n'\times \text{ in } T',\ (n'-1) = (n-1)\frac{T'}{T}

tricks.title: The P r²/10000 gap
tricks.body: For 2 years, the SI–CI difference alone fixes the product structure: two equations, two unknowns.

example.q: The simple interest on a sum for 2 years is ₹800 and the compound interest is ₹832. Find the rate.

tricks.title: Doubling chain at CI
tricks.body: Every T years the money multiplies by the same factor — count the doublings.

example.q: A sum doubles in 8 years at CI. In how many years will it become 8 times?

tricks.title: Difference as first-year interest re-lent
tricks.body: For 2 years, think: $CI - SI$ = (1st year interest) × (R/100).

example.q: The CI–SI difference on a sum for 2 years at 10% is ₹50. Find the sum.

mistakes: Using $P\left(\frac{R}{100}\right)^2$ for 3 years without the $\left(3 + \frac{R}{100}\right)$ factor.
Applying the CI doubling chain to SI problems (SI doubles in T ⇒ 4× in 2T is FALSE at SI; it is 3×).
Forgetting to compute SI from the given amounts before using the difference.
Mixing up which of CI/SI is larger — CI is always ≥ SI for T ≥ 1.
subtopics.notes:
### Why CI and SI differ
For the **first** year, CI and SI on the same sum at the same rate are identical. They part ways from the second year: CI earns interest on the earlier interest, SI never does. So the gap is exactly the *interest earned on the accumulated interest*.

### Two years — the one-line formula
The difference is the first year's interest, re-earned once in the second year:
$$CI - SI = P\left(\frac{R}{100}\right)^2$$
₹12,500 at 12%: $12500 \times 0.12^2 = ₹180$.
Reverse: difference ₹50 at 10% → $P = \frac{50 \times 10000}{100} = ₹5{,}000$.
Notice the shape: P × rate-fraction × rate-fraction. The rate fraction $\frac{R}{100}$ appears once per extra year.

### Three years
The second year's interest also re-earns in the third, and the first year's interest re-earns twice:
$$CI - SI = P\left(\frac{R}{100}\right)^2\left(3 + \frac{R}{100}\right)$$
₹10,000 at 10%: $10000 \times 0.01 \times 3.1 = ₹310$.
At small rates the factor is roughly 3 (for 3 years) or 2 (for 2 years) times $\left(\frac{R}{100}\right)^2 P$.

### CI and SI both given
Given both figures for the same sum, the **difference isolates the rate**:
- 2 years: difference $= P\left(\frac{R}{100}\right)^2$ and SI $= \frac{2PR}{100}$ → divide: $\frac{R}{100} = \frac{\text{difference} \times 2}{SI}$ → $R = \frac{200 \times \text{difference}}{SI}$.
SI ₹800, CI ₹820 → $R = \frac{200 \times 20}{800} = 5\%$, then $P = \frac{800 \times 100}{2 \times 5} = ₹8{,}000$.
- Then the CI itself is just SI + difference.

### Doubling chains at CI
At CI a sum multiplies by the same factor every fixed period. If it **doubles in T years**:
- 4 times in 2T, 8 times in 3T — powers of 2.
- "16 times" = $2^4$ → 4T.
₹P doubling in 6 years → 8 times in 18 years. At SI this does **not** work (linear growth: 3 times takes 2T) — check which interest the question uses.

### Multiplier → rate
Amounts given as multiples: "becomes 1.44 times in 2 years at CI" → chip² $= 1.44$ → chip $= 1.2$ → 20%. Common squares: 1.21 → 10%, 1.44 → 20%, 2.25 → 50%; cubes: 1.728 → 20%, 1.331 → 10%.

### A quick worked case
₹8,000 at 5% for 2 years: SI $= 800$, CI $= 8000(1.05^2 - 1) = 820$ — difference ₹20, which is exactly $8000 \times 0.05^2$. Every 2-year question is this single multiplication in disguise; train yourself to see the rate fraction squared.

### Quick revision
- 2 years: $CI - SI = P\left(\frac{R}{100}\right)^2$.
- 3 years: $CI - SI = P\left(\frac{R}{100}\right)^2\left(3 + \frac{R}{100}\right)$.
- Difference and SI given: $R = \frac{200 \times \text{diff}}{SI}$ (2 years), then $P = \frac{100 \times SI}{2R}$.
- CI doubling chain: ×2 in T → ×$2^k$ in kT.
- Multiplier m in 2 years → rate $= 100(\sqrt{m} - 1)$.

patterns.name: CI − SI for 2 years
patterns.howToSpot: Same sum at the same rate for exactly 2 years — find the difference, or the sum from the difference.
patterns.logic:
1. Apply the formula directly for the difference.
2. Reverse: $P = \frac{\text{difference} \times 10000}{R^2}$.
3. Check magnitude: at 10% the difference is only 1% of P.

Why: only the first year's interest is re-earned, once.

example.q: The difference between the compound and simple interest on a sum for 2 years at 10% per annum is ₹50. Find the sum.

patterns.name: CI − SI for 3 years
patterns.howToSpot: 'For 3 years' with both interests asked or their difference.
patterns.logic:
1. Compute $\left(\frac{R}{100}\right)^2$ and multiply by $\left(3 + \frac{R}{100}\right)$.
2. Multiply by P (or divide the difference by this factor to get P).
3. At 10% the factor is 3.1; the difference is 3.1% of P.

Why: two extra 'interest-on-interest' effects stack up in year three.

example.q: The difference between CI and SI on ₹10,000 for 3 years at 10% per annum is:

patterns.name: CI and SI both given — find rate and sum
patterns.howToSpot: Both the SI and the CI (2 or 3 years) are given for the same sum; the rate or the sum is asked.
patterns.logic:
1. Difference = interest-on-interest; SI = n × first-year interest.
2. Divide difference by SI to get $\frac{R}{100n}$; find R.
3. Then $P = \frac{100 \times SI}{nR}$; CI = SI + difference if asked.

Why: both quantities share the same P and first-year interest.

example.q: The simple interest on a sum for 2 years is ₹800 and the compound interest is ₹820. Find the rate per cent.

patterns.name: Doubling chain at CI (powers)
patterns.howToSpot: 'A sum doubles in T years at CI — when is it 4, 8, 16 times?'
patterns.logic:
1. Write the target as a power of 2: 8 = 2³, 16 = 2⁴.
2. Multiply T by that power.
3. At SI the same question gives T × (n − 1) — don't mix the two.

Why: CI multiplies by a constant factor per period.

example.q: A sum doubles itself in 6 years at compound interest. In how many years will it become 8 times itself?

patterns.name: Multiplier in 2 years — root the chip
patterns.howToSpot: 'Becomes 2.25 times / 1.69 times itself in 2 years at CI' — find the rate.
patterns.logic:
1. Take the square root of the multiplier (2 years) or cube root (3 years).
2. Subtract 1 and convert to a per cent.
3. Known pairs: 1.21 → 10%, 1.44 → 20%, 2.25 → 50%; 1.728 → 20% (3 years).

Why: the multiplier is the chip raised to the number of years.

subtopics.title: Equal annual instalments
subtopics.concept:
A loan at interest is cleared by equal instalments at the end of each year. Two clean methods:

**Tabular (works for both SI and CI):** grow the outstanding debt by one year's interest, subtract the instalment, repeat. The last row must reach zero.

**Present value (CI):** with instalment x and rate r, $P = \dfrac{x}{1+\frac{r}{100}} + \dfrac{x}{(1+\frac{r}{100})^2} + \cdots + \dfrac{x}{(1+\frac{r}{100})^n}$.

**Simple-interest shortcut:** $P = nx - \frac{x\,r}{100}\cdot\frac{n(n-1)}{2}$ (each instalment saved earns interest for the years it was NOT outstanding).

CGL numbers are chosen so the tabular method runs on small fractions — do it year by year.

tricks.title: Tabular year-by-year
tricks.body: Grow, subtract, repeat. Two or three rows finish the question.

example.q: A man borrows ₹1,050 at 10% p.a. compound interest and repays it in two equal annual instalments. Find each instalment.

tricks.title: Present-value fraction add
tricks.body: Discount each instalment by $\left(1+\frac{r}{100}\right)^{-k}$ and add.

example.q: $P = \frac{x}{1.1} + \frac{x}{1.21}$ ⇒ x in one line for 2-year cases.

tricks.title: SI instalment formula
tricks.body: Use $P = nx - \frac{xr}{100} \cdot \frac{n(n-1)}{2}$ directly for simple-interest loans.

example.q: ₹1,950 is repaid in two equal annual instalments at 5% per annum simple interest. Find each instalment.

mistakes: Adding a full year's interest on money already repaid (use the outstanding balance, not the original P).
Counting n instalments but compounding only n − 1 times (or the reverse).
In the SI formula, taking $\frac{n(n+1)}{2}$ instead of $\frac{n(n-1)}{2}$.
Forgetting the final row must hit exactly zero — always verify the tabular closure.
subtopics.notes:
### The idea: instalments repay principal plus interest
A loan of P is cleared by **n equal annual instalments** of ₹x paid at the **end** of each year. Each instalment must cover (a) its share of the principal and (b) interest for the time the money stayed with the borrower.

### Present value — the one rule
The instalment paid after k years is worth only $\frac{x}{(1+r)^k}$ **today**, where $r = \frac{R}{100}$. The loan equals the present values of all instalments:
$$P = \frac{x}{1+r} + \frac{x}{(1+r)^2} + \cdots + \frac{x}{(1+r)^n}$$
Take the common denominator and solve for x. At 10% for 2 years:
$$P = x\left(\frac{10}{11} + \frac{100}{121}\right) = \frac{210x}{121}$$
so P = 2,520 → $x = \frac{2520 \times 121}{210} = ₹1{,}452$.
The tabular check: year 1 debt $= 2520 \times 1.1 - 1452 = 1320$; year 2: $1320 \times 1.1 - 1452 = 0$. Zero after the last instalment confirms the answer.

### Ready denominators
| Rate | 2 instalments | 3 instalments |
|---|---|---|
| 10% | $\frac{210}{121}x$ | $\frac{3310}{1331}x$ |
| 20% | $\frac{55}{36}x$ | $\frac{455}{216}x$ |
| 25% | $\frac{36}{25}x$ | $\frac{244}{125}x$ |
Each entry: P = factor × x, so $x = P \div$ factor. Every fraction comes from chips: $\frac{10}{11} + \frac{100}{121}$ etc.

### Simple-interest instalments
Here interest accrues on the **outstanding principal**, but the standard exam shortcut (which is exact for the usual 'interest on whole period deducted' reading) is:
$$P = nx - \frac{r}{100}\,x\,\frac{n(n-1)}{2}$$
The second term knocks off the interest not payable because later instalments return their money earlier. ₹1,200 at 10% in 5 annual instalments: $1200 = 5x - 0.1x \times 10 = 4x$ → x = ₹300.
A tabular SI walk (add interest on the balance, subtract the instalment) must end at zero; use it to verify small cases.

### Hire purchase / down payment
Two shapes:
1. **Balance carried at a rate, cleared by equal instalments** — apply the present-value rule to the *balance*, not the cash price. Cash price 2,500, down 400, balance 2,100 at 10% in 2 instalments: $\frac{210x}{121} = 2100$ → x = ₹1{,}210.
2. **Flat interest on the whole balance**: instalment $= \frac{\text{balance} + \text{balance} \times R \times T/100}{\text{number of instalments}}$. Balance 6,000 at 12% for 1 year in 12 monthly pieces: $\frac{6000 + 720}{12} = ₹560$.

### Present worth of a future payment
The same rule with one term: ₹1,815 due 2 years from now at 10% CI is worth $\frac{1815}{1.21} = ₹1{,}500$ today. Discounting is the reverse of compounding.

### Quick revision
- $P = \sum \frac{x}{(1+r)^k}$ — one equation, one unknown x.
- 10%, 2 years: $P = \frac{210x}{121}$; 20%: $\frac{55x}{36}$; 25%: $\frac{36x}{25}$.
- Verify by the zero-balance table.
- SI shortcut: $P = nx - \frac{rx}{100} \cdot \frac{n(n-1)}{2}$.
- H.P. flat rate: (balance + flat interest) ÷ instalments.
- Present worth = future value ÷ chip.

patterns.name: Two equal annual instalments (CI)
patterns.howToSpot: 'A loan is returned in 2 equal annual instalments of ₹x at R% CI' — find x, or the loan from x.

1. Set chips: 10% → $\frac{10}{11}, \frac{100}{121}$; 20% → $\frac{5}{6}, \frac{25}{36}$; 25% → $\frac{4}{5}, \frac{16}{25}$.
2. Add the two fractions; P = x × their sum.
3. $x = P \times \frac{\text{denominator}}{\text{numerator}}$. Verify with the zero-balance table.

Why: each instalment is discounted for the years it is delayed.

subtopics.title: Finding P, R, T from amount data
subtopics.concept:
The reverse-direction questions give you amounts and ask for the input:

- Amount at CI after T years ⇒ $P = \dfrac{A}{\left(1+\frac{r}{100}\right)^T}$ — divide by the chip chain.
- Amounts after consecutive years at CI give the yearly factor: $\frac{A_{t+1}}{A_t} = 1 + \frac{r}{100}$.
- At SI, consecutive-year amounts differ by the SAME rupee interest — the difference of two consecutive amounts IS the yearly SI, and $\frac{\text{yearly SI}}{P} \times 100$ = rate.
- Two equations (2-year and 3-year amounts) solve for P and R simultaneously.

mistakes: Using T years of SI data in a CI formula (check: SI amounts grow additively).
For consecutive amounts, subtracting when you must divide (CI) or dividing when you must subtract (SI).
Answering the rate as the chip (1.1) instead of 10%.
In two-amount problems, forgetting to verify P comes out positive and sensible.
subtopics.notes:
### Reading rates out of amounts
When a sum **amounts** to given figures after whole years, the *growth between consecutive years* tells the story.

### At compound interest — the ratio trick
Consecutive yearly amounts differ by the year's interest, and
$$\frac{A_{T+1}}{A_T} = 1 + \frac{R}{100}$$
Amounts ₹4,840 (after 2 years) and ₹5,324 (after 3 years): $\frac{5324}{4840} = 1.1$ → 10%. The principal itself is not needed. From the rate, walk back to P: $\frac{4840}{1.21} = ₹4{,}000$.

### At simple interest — the constant difference
SI adds the **same rupees** every year, so consecutive amounts differ by exactly one year's interest:
$$A_{T+1} - A_T = \frac{PR}{100}$$
₹4,500 and ₹5,000: yearly interest ₹500; the sum at the start $= 4500 - 500 = ₹4{,}000$; rate $= \frac{500 \times 100}{4000} = 12.5\%$.
Non-consecutive years: divide the amount gap by the year gap first. ₹6,800 in 3 years and ₹8,000 in 5 years → $\frac{8000 - 6800}{2} = ₹600$ per year.

### Two SIs on one sum
If the SI for 2 years is 1,200 and for 3 years 1,800, the difference (₹600) is one year's interest — and $\frac{PR}{100} = 600$. That is one equation in two unknowns, so the question must supply P or R as well: P ₹10,000 → rate 6%; rate 6% → P ₹10,000. The two SIs together never determine both by themselves.

### Amounts spanning 2y and 3y at SI — the classic pair
'A sum amounts to A in 2 years and B in 3 years at SI':
yearly interest $= B - A$; P $= A - 2(B - A) = 3A - 2B$; rate $= \frac{(B-A) \times 100}{P}$.
₹5,200 (3 years) and ₹5,600 (4 years): yearly ₹400, P $= 5200 - 3 \times 400 = ₹4{,}000$, rate 10%.

### Finding P from an amount at CI
Divide by the chips: amount ₹6,655 after 3 years at 10% → $\frac{6655}{1.331} = ₹5{,}000$. Recognise $1.1^3 = 1.331$, $1.1^2 = 1.21$, $1.2^2 = 1.44$, $1.25^2 = 1.5625$.

### A quick worked case
CI, amounts 4,840 → 5,324: ratio 1.1, so 10% — and P $= \frac{4840}{1.21} = ₹4{,}000$ if asked. The same pair at SI would mean yearly interest ₹484, P $= 4356$, rate $= \frac{48400}{4356} = 11\frac{1}{9}\%$ — different answers from the same numbers, because the growth laws differ. Decide CI or SI first; the reading of the gap depends on it.

### Where the marks go
- Reading a CI gap as a rupee amount (it grows every year) or an SI gap as a ratio (it is constant) — the two standard swaps.
- Forgetting to divide non-consecutive gaps by the year count: 3 → 5 years is TWO years of interest.
- Discounting only once from a 3-year amount, or compounding when the question says simple.

### Quick revision
- CI: $\frac{A_{T+1}}{A_T} = 1 + \frac{R}{100}$ — rate needs no P.
- SI: $A_{T+1} - A_T = $ one year's interest, constant every year.
- Non-consecutive: divide the gap by the year gap.
- P from SI amounts: subtract the accrued interest years × yearly interest.
- P from CI amounts: divide by the chip power.

patterns.name: Principal from an amount at CI
patterns.howToSpot: An amount after 2 or 3 whole years at a known CI rate is given; the original sum is asked.
patterns.logic:
1. Recall the chip powers: $1.1^2 = 1.21$, $1.1^3 = 1.331$, $1.2^2 = 1.44$.
2. Divide the amount by the right power.
3. Sanity check: P must be smaller than the amount.

Why: discounting undoes the compounding exactly.

patterns.name: Rate from consecutive CI amounts
patterns.howToSpot: Amounts after T and T+1 years are given at CI; the rate is asked.
patterns.logic:
1. Divide the later amount by the earlier one.
2. Subtract 1 and read the rate.
3. If P is asked, discount the given amount by the chips.

Why: one year of growth is exactly one chip.

patterns.name: Rate from consecutive SI amounts
patterns.howToSpot: Amounts after T and T+1 years at SI; the rate (or the sum) is asked.
patterns.logic:
1. The difference is one year's interest — constant at SI.
2. Subtract it from the earlier amount to get P.
3. Rate = difference ÷ P × 100.

Why: SI growth is arithmetic, so equal gaps hold equal interest.

example.q: A sum amounts to ₹4,500 in 1 year and ₹5,000 in 2 years at simple interest. Find the rate per annum.

patterns.name: Amounts spanning several years at SI
patterns.howToSpot: 'Amounts to A in m years and B in n years (m ≠ n ± 1)' — or two SIs over different periods.
patterns.logic:
1. Divide the amount gap by the year gap.
2. P = A − m × yearly interest.
3. Rate = yearly ÷ P × 100. For two plain SIs, the difference of the SIs over 1 year is the yearly interest.

Why: the linear growth makes any two points fix the line.

example.q: A sum amounts to ₹6,800 in 3 years and ₹8,000 in 5 years at simple interest. Find the rate per annum.

patterns.name: Two SIs on the same sum
patterns.howToSpot: 'SI for 2 years is x, for 3 years is y' — the difference pins the yearly interest; P or R comes from the question.
patterns.logic:
1. Yearly interest = difference of the two SIs ÷ year gap.
2. The yearly figure equals $\frac{PR}{100}$ — one equation. If the question gives P, get R; if it gives R, get P.
3. Check by recomputing both SIs.

Why: same sum, same rate — every extra year adds the same rupees.

pyqPatterns.approach: SI = PRT/100; if an amount is given take SI = A − P first. 'n times in T years' gives R = 100(n−1)/T — the interest is only (n−1) times the principal.

pyqPatterns.approach: 2 years: P(R/100)². 3 years: P(R/100)²(3 + R/100). Reverse the factor to get P. With both CI and SI given, R = 200 × difference/SI for 2 years.

pyqPatterns.howToSpot: 'Compounded half-yearly or quarterly', usually for 1–2 years including halves like 1½ years.
pyqPatterns.approach: Halve the rate and double the periods (quarter them for quarterly): A = P(1 + R/200)^(2T). Count periods carefully — 1½ years half-yearly is 3 periods.

pyqPatterns.approach: CI: powers of 2 — 8 times in 3T. SI: linear — (n−1) rule, R = 100(n−1)/T. Mixing the two growth laws is the trap.

pyqPatterns.approach: Discount each instalment: P = Σ x/(1+r)^k. 10%, 2 years: P = 210x/121. Verify with a zero-balance table. SI version: P = nx − (r/100)x·n(n−1)/2.

pyqPatterns.approach: Multiply year-wise chips: A = P(1+r₁)(1+r₂). A negative year (loss) uses its own chip. Never average the rates.
